tagline: Rolling roads connect Missouri River towns across hills carved by glaciers.
intro: The Glacial Hills Scenic Byway rolls through northeastern Kansas for 63 miles between the Nebraska border and Leavenworth. Kansas Tourism emphasizes hills and rock-strewn valleys carved by glaciers, then shaped by wind and rain. The route follows K-7 with a county-road diversion near Troy. Along the northern stretch, the highway closely parallels the Missouri River; farther south, Atchison occupies its western bank. Between Atchison and Leavenworth, K-7 shares the road with US 73.

K-7 did not originally reach this far north. Designated in 1927, it first ended west of Kansas City. In 1933–34, the highway extended along the former K-16 to Troy. Approval for another extension came in 1935, and by 1937 the section from Sparks to the Nebraska border was complete. The numbered highway thus reached towns that had already developed around steamboat traffic at White Cloud and the westbound wagon route through Troy.

Driving south, begin at the Nebraska line near White Cloud and follow K-7 toward Troy. The byway uses 195th Road, Last Chance Road and 180th Road near Troy before returning to K-7. Continue to Atchison, where a former Santa Fe freight depot houses the county historical museum, then finish at K-92 near Fort Leavenworth’s gates.

moments.title: White Cloud
moments.text: White Cloud’s downtown overlooks the Missouri River, the waterway whose steamboat traffic helped the town prosper. Land promoters John Utt and Enoch Spaulding bought the townsite in 1857 and sold lots. The downtown historic district includes Italianate, Gothic Revival and Greek Revival architecture. A different piece of local history belongs to ten-year-old Wilbur Chapman: in 1913 he raised a pig, sold it for $25 and donated the proceeds to the American Mission to Lepers. An obelisk-shaped monument was installed in his honor in front of Community Christian Church. White Cloud is the seat of government for the Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska.

moments.title: Troy
moments.text: Troy grew beside the wagon route from St. Joseph to Oregon and California. Platted in 1855, it had its first house the following year and its first store in 1857. The county seat’s courthouse represents a later phase of building: completed in 1906, it was Doniphan County’s fourth courthouse. Architect George P. Washburn gave the red-brick building a limestone base and circular towers at every corner. Above them rises a ten-sided cupola. On the top floor, a stone band connects the arched windows, a precise detail to pick out from the courthouse square.
moments.notice: At the courthouse, look for circular corner towers and arched upper windows linked by a stone band.

moments.title: Atchison
moments.text: Atchison was the original eastern terminus of the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway, but the connection to Topeka took time. Construction began in Topeka in 1868, headed west and south; the link back to Atchison was not completed until May 1872. The city’s railroad story now has a home in the 1880 Santa Fe Freight Depot, where the Atchison County Historical Society moved its museum in 1989. Its exhibits include railroad history and aviator Amelia Earhart. Elsewhere in this Missouri River city, the Amelia Earhart Birthplace Museum provides another connection to her life.
